claims.text: Enhancing chemical short-range order stabilizes a single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy.
Enhanced short-range order reinforces interatomic bonding.
Enhanced short-range order inhibits diffusion-driven nucleation of deleterious secondary phases.
Short-range-order-induced phase stabilization retains high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Rapid quenching can produce a single-phase FCC or BCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a relatively disordered atomic configuration.
Controlled aging at 600–750 °C promotes short-range-order development in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
The spatial extent and distribution of short-range-order clusters modify local interatomic bonding.
Short-range-order clusters reduce the thermodynamic driving force for secondary-phase nucleation.
Short-range-order stabilization delays or suppresses diffusion-controlled phase transformations during high-temperature exposure, irradiation, and cryogenic conditions.
Aged, short-range-order-enhanced samples will form secondary phases more slowly or in smaller quantities than rapidly quenched samples.
Aged samples will have higher high-temperature strength than rapidly quenched samples.
Aged samples will maintain greater radiation tolerance than rapidly quenched samples.
Aged samples will have greater cryogenic toughness than rapidly quenched samples.
A rapidly quenched, largely disordered Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline is more prone to thermal- or irradiation-induced phase transformation.
Excessive grain growth or coarsening during aging may negate the proposed stabilization effect.
The magnitude of the proposed stabilization and mechanical-property effects may depend sensitively on aging time, aging temperature, and subsequent operating conditions.
